objectives.title: Custom Connectors & Azure Integration
objectives.summary: Ordering an Entra-Graph custom connector integration (register, permission, consent, connect, call), separating Dataverse event delivery from Azure Function ETL compute, and reasoning about the effective DLP policy that governs which connectors an app or flow may combine.

objectives.title: Dataverse Extensibility & Platform Limits
objectives.summary: Designing a Dataverse document architecture within platform storage limits (SharePoint binaries, alternate-key matching, recoverable batch compute) and building delegable canvas-app queries that respect delegation limits with correct date-window boundaries.

questions.prompt: Which order correctly prepares a Canvas app to call Graph through a custom connector on behalf of its signed-in user?

options.text: Register → Permission → Consent → Connect → Call
Consent → Register → Call → Permission → Connect
Connect → Register → Consent → Permission → Call
Call → Connect → Permission → Consent → Register

questions.rationale: The registration gives the connector identity; permissions are requested on it; consent approves them; connector configuration uses that identity; then the app calls it.

questions.prompt: Why must consent follow Graph permission configuration?

options.text: Consent creates the app registration
Consent assigns the user a directory role
Consent creates the Canvas app
Consent approves requested access; without a request there is nothing to approve

questions.rationale: Permission and consent are separate: permissions declare what the application requests, while consent authorizes that request.

questions.prompt: What permission mode best fits a Canvas app checking the currently logged-in user's membership through Graph?

options.text: No OAuth permissions
Dataverse table permissions
Delegated permissions
Application permissions

questions.rationale: The connector is acting on behalf of a signed-in user. Application permissions are for app-only background/daemon work.

questions.prompt: What does the custom connector contribute to this design?

options.text: Replacement for server-side authorization
A reusable OAuth/Graph operation contract that the Canvas app can call
Automatic assignment of Global Administrator to every user
Replacement for consent

questions.rationale: The connector encapsulates OAuth and API plumbing. It does not grant directory roles, consent, or protected-operation authorization.

questions.prompt: Which statement distinguishes role, permission, and consent correctly?

options.text: Role is user authority; permission is app-requested API access; consent approves that request
All three are the same tenant setting
Consent assigns every user the role
A Graph permission automatically shares the Canvas app

questions.rationale: These are separate controls and must not be collapsed into one authorization concept.

questions.prompt: A Canvas app hides its user-management screen for non-admins. What additional control is required?

options.text: Nothing; hidden UI is enforcement
Make every user a Global Administrator
Store the role in a screen variable only
The protected API/backend independently validates authorization

questions.rationale: Client-side navigation is not a security boundary. The protected operation must enforce authorization.

questions.prompt: What changes if a nightly background job, with no signed-in user, calls Graph?

options.text: Remove consent
Call Graph directly from a Canvas screen
Evaluate application permissions and app-only authorization instead of delegated user access
Keep delegated permissions because every API needs a user

questions.rationale: No signed-in user changes the runtime identity model. Background jobs normally use app-only/application permissions, with corresponding consent and least-privilege design.

questions.prompt: In a Webhook + Azure Function integration, which component performs custom transformation logic?

options.text: Azure Function
Webhook
Dataverse Web API
Web resource

questions.rationale: The webhook delivers a Dataverse event to an external endpoint. The Azure Function is the custom compute layer that maps, validates, cleanses, or converts the payload/data.

questions.prompt: What is the normal direction of a Dataverse webhook?

options.text: External legacy application → Dataverse scheduler
Browser web resource → server-side migration job
Microsoft Graph → any arbitrary legacy system
Dataverse server event → external handler

questions.rationale: Dataverse webhooks send server events outward as POST JSON payloads to an external web application. That direction is the production-design check that qualifies the exam answer.

questions.prompt: Why is Web Resource + Dataverse Web API a poor fit for a transformation-heavy background migration?

options.text: The Dataverse Web API cannot create or update rows
Web resources run as Azure Functions automatically
The web resource is browser-processed UI code, while the Web API is a data endpoint rather than an ETL engine
Web resources cannot contain JavaScript

questions.rationale: Web resources are static HTML, JavaScript, CSS, image, and related browser assets used to extend model-driven apps. The Web API can perform data operations, but neither component independently supplies a reliable server-side ETL pipeline.

questions.prompt: An Account update in Dataverse must invoke custom code that enriches the data and writes selected results to another system. Which trace best fits?

options.text: Account update → Microsoft Graph → arbitrary legacy application
Dataverse Account update → registered webhook → Azure Function handler → external/Dataverse API calls
Account update → web resource server code → automatic background load
Account update → custom connector definition with no caller → migration completes

questions.rationale: This is a Dataverse-originated event. Register a webhook step, host the handler such as an Azure Function, and let the Function perform custom processing and necessary API calls.

questions.prompt: What is the most accurate role of a custom connector in an integration design?

options.text: It defines how apps, flows, and other supported consumers call an API's operations and security
It automatically schedules and reconciles every legacy-data migration
It is a model-driven app browser UI file
It is the Dataverse server event that POSTs to an endpoint

questions.rationale: Custom connectors describe API operations, data structures, and authentication for consumers such as Power Apps and Power Automate. They can be part of a design but are not synonymous with a webhook, Function, or ETL orchestration runtime.

questions.prompt: A Dataverse event stream could overwhelm a direct HTTP handler and requires durable buffering. Which integration comparison matters most?

options.text: Replace the Function with a web resource because web resources run offline
Use Microsoft Graph because it queues Dataverse events
Use a custom connector because it guarantees durable event delivery
Consider Azure Service Bus because it provides queuing for high-scale processing

questions.rationale: Microsoft documents Azure Service Bus as providing a full queuing mechanism for high-scale Dataverse event processing. Direct webhooks scale only to the capacity of the receiving hosted service.

questions.prompt: What changes when the requirement becomes a nightly one-time-style pull from legacy systems into Dataverse, with no Dataverse event starting the work?

options.text: Move the migration into a web resource so it runs in the model-driven browser
Use Microsoft Graph regardless of what the legacy source exposes
Use a timer, pipeline, dataflow, or equivalent external trigger; retain an Azure Function only where custom transformation is needed
Register a Dataverse webhook because every Dataverse migration begins with a server event

questions.rationale: The delivery/orchestration mechanism must match the origin. A Dataverse webhook is outbound notification from a Dataverse event; a scheduled legacy migration needs a scheduler or pipeline outside that event path. Custom compute may still be an Azure Function.

questions.prompt: Across multiple applicable data policies, which connector classification has unconditional precedence?

options.text: Blocked
Business
Non-Business
The classification in the newest policy

questions.rationale: If any applicable tenant-level or environment-level policy marks a connector Blocked, no app or flow can use that connector in the environment. Other Business or Non-Business classifications do not override it.

questions.prompt: What does a Business or Non-Business classification primarily establish?

options.text: A ranking of connector security quality
A license tier for the connector
A precedence rule based on policy creation time
A data-sharing boundary that controls which connectors may be used together

questions.rationale: Business and Non-Business are separation groups. The important question is whether connectors remain grouped together across every applicable policy, not whether one label sounds more trusted.

questions.prompt: Policy A groups SharePoint and Salesforce as Business. Policy B groups SharePoint as Business and Salesforce as Non-Business. Why can they not coexist in one flow?

options.text: Policy B is necessarily newer than Policy A
SharePoint can never be combined with Salesforce
Their complete fingerprints differ: [Business, Business] versus [Business, Non-Business]
Non-Business connectors are always blocked

questions.rationale: The policies are intersected. Sharing a group under Policy A is insufficient because Policy B separates the connectors. Non-Business is not itself Blocked.

questions.prompt: Three applicable policies classify Outlook as [Business, Business, Business] and SharePoint as [Business, Business, Non-Business]. What is the effective relationship?

options.text: The tenant-level classification must be discarded
They occupy different effective groups and cannot be mixed in one resource
They are compatible because two of three policies agree
SharePoint is Blocked because one position is Non-Business

questions.rationale: Compatibility requires equality at every position; this is not majority voting. Non-Business means a different group, not Blocked, and applicable tenant/environment classifications are not discarded by scope hierarchy.

questions.prompt: A maker adds a conflicting connector pair to a cloud flow and selects Save. Which outcome best matches Power Automate design-time enforcement?

options.text: The flow can be saved but is marked Suspended and will not execute until the violation is resolved
The flow runs once and is then permanently deleted
The newest policy is ignored until the next solution import
Only the connector action fails while the rest of the flow executes

questions.rationale: Power Automate can save the flow, but a data-policy violation causes it to be marked Suspended and prevents execution until the maker resolves the conflict.

questions.prompt: An existing flow became noncompliant after an admin changed a policy, but its status has not changed immediately. What is the best first interpretation?

options.text: DLP applies only during design and can never affect an existing flow
The environment-level policy automatically canceled the tenant-level policy
A saved flow is permanently exempt from later policy changes
Runtime suspension uses a background polling process, so enforcement status may take time to update

questions.rationale: Existing resources are evaluated against the latest applicable policies, but the flow/app suspension process works in polling mode. A short delay alone does not prove that the policy is ineffective.

questions.prompt: A flow uses SharePoint [Business, Business] and Salesforce [Business, Non-Business]. What changes if Policy B is narrowed so it no longer applies to the flow's environment, while Policy A still applies and neither connector is Blocked?

options.text: Salesforce remains Blocked because Non-Business is irreversible
Policy A is ignored because it has fewer classifications
The remaining fingerprints both become [Business], so this particular DLP grouping conflict is removed
Nothing changes because every policy ever created remains permanent

questions.rationale: Scope determines which policies participate. Once Policy B no longer applies, both connectors have the same remaining fingerprint under Policy A. That removes this grouping conflict, although authorization, connection health, and other applicable controls still require separate validation.

questions.prompt: Which component should store the large collection of customer documents for native model-driven record-context document management?

options.text: SharePoint
Dataverse Notes
Dataverse Web API
Azure Function memory

questions.rationale: SharePoint stores and manages documents in the context of model-driven app records. The Web API matches business records; Notes are not the best large-repository choice.

questions.prompt: What is the correct responsibility split in the selected architecture?

options.text: Web API migrates and stores every file; SharePoint only authenticates
Notes store binaries; C# is only a UI extension
Power Automate supplies all required checkpointing automatically
C# migrates; Web API matches Dataverse customers; SharePoint stores files

questions.rationale: Separate compute, business-record lookup, and document storage. The source system, Dataverse, and SharePoint each have distinct responsibilities.

questions.prompt: The Oracle customer number is stable but the Dataverse account GUID is unknown. What is the strongest matching design?

options.text: Create a new account for every document
Put the Oracle number in a browser web resource
Define/use a Dataverse alternate key and query it through the Web API or SDK
Match only on account name

questions.rationale: Alternate keys support integration operations when the primary GUID is not known. A stable external ID avoids fragile name matching.

questions.prompt: Why is a C# console application preferred over a cloud flow for this stated initial migration?

options.text: It automatically gives every user SharePoint access
It gives explicit batching, checkpoint, retry, logging, and reconciliation control
Cloud flows can never call SharePoint
Only console apps can call the Dataverse Web API

questions.rationale: The requirement is high-volume and initial. Code provides direct operational control; this does not mean flows are impossible or never appropriate.

questions.prompt: Why is Azure Blob Storage not the best selected answer here?

options.text: It lacks SharePoint's standard model-driven document-management experience without custom UI/integration
Blob Storage cannot store documents
Blob Storage always consumes Dataverse database capacity
Blob Storage cannot be accessed from C#

questions.rationale: Blob Storage is technically capable, but standard Dynamics/model-driven customer-document experience points to SharePoint integration unless the team deliberately builds the custom layer.

questions.prompt: What changes if new documents arrive one at a time after migration in a modest-volume business process?

options.text: Move all documents into Notes
Replace SharePoint with the Dataverse Web API
Remove customer matching because the process is ongoing
Power Automate may now be a reasonable orchestrator, while SharePoint storage and Dataverse customer matching remain separate concerns

questions.rationale: The workload shape changes the orchestration choice. It does not change SharePoint's document role or the need to associate a document with the correct Dataverse customer.

questions.prompt: Which function returns the collection of matching records a gallery Items property needs?

options.text: Filter
LookUp
DateDiff
Set

questions.rationale: Filter returns a table containing every record that satisfies the condition. LookUp returns one record; DateDiff returns a number; Set changes state but returns no value.

questions.prompt: Why can storing the DateAdd result in DateDuration help with the stated delegation warning?

options.text: It makes all Power Fx functions delegable
It converts Shipping Date into a text column
It makes LookUp return a table
It leaves a simple column-to-scalar predicate for the connector to evaluate if supported

questions.rationale: The intended pattern calculates a scalar once, then sends Shipping Date <= DateDuration. Delegation still must be verified for the actual data source and column.

questions.prompt: What kind of value does DateDiff(Now(), Today(), Minutes) return?

options.text: A table of orders
The current time
A number of minutes
A future date

questions.rationale: DateDiff returns a whole number of the requested units between two date/time values. It cannot supply a date boundary for Shipping Date.

questions.prompt: Where is the correct place to execute Set(DateDuration, DateAdd(Today(), 7, Days))?

options.text: Inside LookUp so it returns a table
Screen.OnVisible or another behavior property
Gallery.Items as a separate statement
A gallery template label's Text property

questions.rationale: Set is a behavior function and has no return value. Run it from a behavior property, then reference DateDuration from Gallery.Items.

questions.prompt: Which pair is the keyed answer for the exam scenario?

options.text: Set(DateDuration, DateAdd(Today(), 7, Days)); then Filter(Orders, 'Shipping Date' <= DateDuration)
Set(DateDuration, DateDiff(Now(), Today(), Minutes)); then LookUp(Orders, 'Shipping Date' = DateDuration)
Filter(Orders, 'Shipping Date' = Today()); then Set(Orders, DateDuration)
LookUp(Orders, 'Shipping Date' <= DateDuration); then DateAdd(Orders, 7, Days)

questions.rationale: This pair creates the future cutoff and returns all orders through it. It is the keyed MeasureUp solution; production wording may require a lower boundary too.

questions.prompt: Why is a delegation warning a correctness concern for a large Orders source?

options.text: The gallery will show every row twice
DateAdd will change into DateDiff
Set variables are automatically deleted
Power Apps can evaluate the filter over only a limited local subset, omitting qualifying rows

questions.rationale: When delegation is not possible, Power Apps retrieves a limited set of records and evaluates locally. The gallery can therefore look plausible while missing results.

questions.prompt: The requirement changes: Shipping Date is a date-time column, and the gallery must include every order from today through the end of the seventh day. What is the strongest pattern?

options.text: Use LookUp with Shipping Date = EndExclusive
Use DateDiff as the Shipping Date value
Set StartDate to Today and EndExclusive to DateAdd(StartDate, 8, Days), then Filter with Shipping Date >= StartDate && Shipping Date < EndExclusive
Keep only Shipping Date <= DateAdd(Today(), 7, Days)

questions.rationale: An exclusive boundary at the start of day eight includes the entire seventh day without relying on an ambiguous end-of-day timestamp. Confirm that the predicates delegate for the real source.

misconceptions.name: OAuth chain as a checklist
misconceptions.contrast: Consent approves an already-requested permission, and each stage of Register, Permission, Consent, Connect, Call depends on the one before it. The chain is a dependency order, not an unordered setup checklist.
socraticSeeds: Which stage produces the thing that consent approves?
What breaks first if you try to grant consent before any permission is requested?

misconceptions.name: Permission mode chosen by data sensitivity
misconceptions.contrast: A signed-in Canvas user normally implies delegated access; application permissions fit unattended daemon and background processes. The caller identity, not how privileged the data feels, selects the permission mode.
socraticSeeds: Who is present at runtime when this call executes?
Does privileged data change who the caller is?

misconceptions.name: Role, permission, and consent collapsed
misconceptions.contrast: A directory role is assigned to a user; a Graph permission is requested by an app; consent approves the app request. They are separate controls and must not be merged into one authorization concept.
socraticSeeds: Which of these belongs to the user, and which to the app?
What exactly does consent approve?

misconceptions.name: Client code as a server boundary
misconceptions.contrast: Hiding a screen or running browser JavaScript is user experience, not enforcement or compute. Web resources have no server-side execution capability, and a protected operation must validate authorization independently even if a user bypasses client navigation.
socraticSeeds: If a user bypasses the app navigation, what still stops the operation?
Where does this code actually execute?

misconceptions.name: One component absorbs every job
misconceptions.contrast: A webhook is event delivery; the Azure Function is custom compute; the Web API loads data; a custom connector describes how consumers call an API. No component absorbs its neighbor’s job, and the first component in a diagram is not automatically the one doing the processing.
socraticSeeds: Which single job does this component actually own?
Which component in your design is quietly doing two jobs?

misconceptions.name: Trigger chosen without naming the event origin
misconceptions.contrast: Dataverse webhooks originate from Dataverse server events and send them outward. A scheduled pull from legacy systems needs a timer, pipeline, dataflow, or source-side trigger; the delivery mechanism must match where the event starts.
socraticSeeds: Which system creates the event that starts this work?
What fires first on the night this migration runs?

misconceptions.name: Cloud flow as a bulk migration engine
misconceptions.contrast: A high-volume initial migration needs controlled batching, checkpoints, retries, reconciliation, and restartability that a purpose-built batch application handles more directly. Cloud flows fit modest, event-driven ongoing workloads.
socraticSeeds: What happens to this run at file 40,000 of 100,000 when a call fails?
How does this workload resume after a failure?

misconceptions.name: One policy wins by precedence
misconceptions.contrast: Power Platform evaluates all applicable data policies together. Neither nearest scope nor most-recent edit creates an override: Blocked takes precedence, and Business/Non-Business groupings intersect across every applicable policy.
socraticSeeds: Which policies participate for this environment, and what says one of them outranks another?
What result do you get if no policy wins and all of them apply?

misconceptions.name: Business as a permission rank
misconceptions.contrast: Business and Non-Business are separation groups, not allow-and-deny levels or quality ratings. Compatibility depends on whether two connectors stay grouped together under every applicable policy, and Non-Business is not Blocked.
socraticSeeds: Is Business allowing something, or grouping something?
What would “more permissive” even mean for a data-boundary label?

misconceptions.name: One policy view looks conclusive
misconceptions.contrast: Two unblocked connectors must share the same classification fingerprint across all applicable policies. Sharing a group in one policy, or in a majority of policies, is insufficient: a mismatch in any single policy separates them.
socraticSeeds: Which other policies also classify these two connectors?
What does the full fingerprint look like, position by position?

misconceptions.name: DLP checks only at save time
misconceptions.contrast: Data policies are enforced at runtime too: existing apps and flows can become noncompliant after a policy change, a violating flow saves but is marked Suspended and will not execute, and suspension uses background polling so it may not be instantaneous.
socraticSeeds: What happens to a flow that was compliant when it was saved?
If the status has not changed yet, has enforcement actually failed?

misconceptions.name: It can store the bytes, so it fits
misconceptions.contrast: Raw capability is not fit. Blob Storage needs a custom record-to-blob experience, and Notes consume Dataverse capacity and lack document-management strengths; SharePoint provides the standard document experience in model-driven record context.
socraticSeeds: What experience must users get when they open the record?
What does this choice cost in capacity or custom UI to reach that experience?

misconceptions.name: Record matching on mutable names
misconceptions.contrast: An alternate key on a stable source identifier resolves the right record when the Dataverse GUID is unknown. Display names are mutable and fragile, and dropping the match entirely orphans documents from their business records.
socraticSeeds: What happens when two accounts share a name, or one is renamed?
Which identifier survives every rename?

misconceptions.name: Function chosen by keyword, not return type
misconceptions.contrast: Filter returns a table of all matching rows; LookUp returns one record; DateAdd returns a date/time; DateDiff returns a number of units; Set returns no value. The return type decides where each function can be used.
socraticSeeds: What type of value does this property need?
What exactly does that function hand back?

misconceptions.name: Set inside a data formula
misconceptions.contrast: Set is a behavior-only function with no return value, and its variable does not automatically recalculate. Gallery.Items is a data formula that must evaluate to a table: run Set from a behavior property and reference the variable.
socraticSeeds: Does this property run actions, or evaluate to a value?
What would Gallery.Items display if its formula returns nothing?

misconceptions.name: Delegation as a generic function property
misconceptions.contrast: Delegation is connector-, operator-, and column-type-specific. A delegation warning means the app may evaluate the predicate over a limited local subset and silently omit qualifying rows; it must be verified against the actual data source.
socraticSeeds: Which connector, operator, and column type is this predicate actually hitting?
How would you notice if qualifying rows were missing?

misconceptions.name: An upper bound treated as a window
misconceptions.contrast: An upper bound alone admits every older row. A true next-seven-days window needs both boundaries, and for date-time data an exclusive next-day upper bound is what covers all of day seven.
socraticSeeds: What is the oldest order this filter admits?
Which orders on day seven itself does your boundary include?
